clue.text: Scholarly rascal consumed by a terrible malice

indicators.note: what is consumed ends up inside whatever eats it, so one piece goes within the other
something terrible is in a bad way, so the following words are knocked out of their order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
a cad is a dishonourable man, a rascal

explanation.surface: A learned academic villain is swallowed up by spite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scholarly rascal' reads as one person, but the adjective is the definition and the rascal goes inside the jumble after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Academical is an older adjective for things relating to a university or to learning, close to scholarly.

clue.text: Gathers American is supported by fools

parts.note: AM is a standard abbreviation for American
asses are fools

explanation.surface: An American gathering things, propped up by idiots.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer, 'supported by' puts the fools underneath the American.
explanation.definitionFit: To amass is to collect or accumulate, so amasses is a verb form matching gathers.

clue.text: Gunners behind on table at regular intervals

parts.note: arse is British slang for the backside

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals means picking every other one from the phrase

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Arsenal fans trail at the bottom of the league table.
explanation.walkthrough: The Gunners is the nickname of Arsenal, the London football club; 'behind' looks like a league position but is the slang word for a bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: Arsenal Football Club is nicknamed the Gunners after its origins at the Royal Arsenal munitions works.

clue.text: Stranger with additional lager possibly losing head

indicators.note: losing its head means the word drops its first letter

parts.note: lager is one kind of beer, so with more of it something is beerier

explanation.surface: Things get weirder once someone has had extra lager.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' marks lager as an example of beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Eerie means uncanny or weird, so eerier is a comparative meaning odder or stranger.

clue.text: Drinking establishments popular with empty nesters

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular

indicators.note: an emptied word has its insides removed, leaving only the two outside letters

parts.note: the first and last letters

explanation.surface: Pubs are a favourite with parents whose children have left home.
explanation.definitionFit: Inns are traditional pubs or taverns where drink is served, often with lodging too.

clue.text: Area 51 ultimately wore down extraterrestrial

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for area
LI is 51 in Roman numerals

indicators.note: ultimately points at the final letter of each of the following words

parts.note: the last letter of each word

explanation.surface: Area 51, the secret US base, finally wore down a visitor from space.
explanation.walkthrough: Area 51 is famous for alien legends, so the solver reads it as one place; it splits into an abbreviation and a Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: An alien is a being from another world, which is what extraterrestrial means as a noun.

clue.text: Boss getting apprentices half-cut

indicators.note: cut by half means only the front half of the word survives

parts.note: apprentices are learners, students

explanation.surface: A manager finds the trainees drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: Half-cut is British slang for tipsy, which is the picture; here it means cut in half. A boss is a raised knob on a surface, as is a stud.
explanation.definitionFit: A boss is an ornamental raised knob, for example on a shield, which is also called a stud.

clue.text: A couple of syllables to cheer when throwing up a drop of red

indicators.text: when throwing up a drop of red
indicators.note: in a down entry, throwing up the first letter of red lifts that one letter higher, rearranging the phrase

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone cheers, then vomits up a drop of red wine.
explanation.walkthrough: The R at the end of TO CHEER moves up to second place. 'Throwing up' paints vomiting, but in a down clue it means moving upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A trochee is a metrical foot of two syllables, stressed then unstressed, as in 'happy'.

clue.text: New nans due to become responsible older women

indicators.note: making something new means remaking it, so the letters come out in a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Newly minted grandmothers are set to take charge.
explanation.walkthrough: Nan is British for grandmother.
explanation.definitionFit: A duenna is an older woman employed as chaperone or governess to girls in a Spanish or Portuguese family.

clue.text: Loser's lesion oddly covered in distinctive sort of stitches

indicators.note: being covered in something means sitting wrapped inside it

parts.note: Aran is a knitting style with distinctive cable stitches, from the Aran Islands

indicators.note: oddly means taking the letters in odd-numbered positions

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: A loser has a sore that has been stitched up oddly.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay. Stitches suggests surgery, but it is knitting.
explanation.definitionFit: An also-ran is a horse that finishes unplaced, and by extension anyone who fails to win.

clue.text: I like this drink which may be radioactive

definitions.note: a description of the answer rather than a noun

parts.note: taken as written
so means in this way
to tope is to drink alcohol heavily

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys a drink that turns out to be radioactive.
explanation.definitionFit: An isotope is a form of an element with a different number of neutrons, and some isotopes are radioactive.

clue.text: Drug cops did lates with absolutely no cover

indicators.note: stripping every word of its cover means removing the outside letters, keeping only the middles

parts.note: without first and last letters
without first and last letters
without first and last letters

explanation.surface: Police worked late shifts on a drugs case with no undercover officers.
explanation.definitionFit: An opiate is a drug derived from opium, such as morphine or codeine.

clue.text: Twisted menace behaved wickedly

indicators.note: twisted round means turned to face the other way, so the name is read backwards

parts.note: Dennis the Menace is a mischievous boy in the British comic The Beano

explanation.surface: A warped threat acted badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twisted' wants to be an anagram signal, but the letters are simply reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: To sin is to commit a moral wrong, so sinned is a past tense verb matching behaved wickedly.

clue.text: Words recited in panto, perhaps, when horse enters

indicators.note: something that enters goes inside the other letters
perhaps signals one possible arrangement of the letters before it

parts.note: taken as written
horse is slang for heroin, whose abbreviation is H

explanation.surface: Lines spoken in a pantomime when the pantomime horse comes on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: A panto is a British Christmas stage show, often with a two-person horse costume, which is the false picture.
explanation.definitionFit: An antiphon is a verse or response sung or recited alternately by two groups, as in church services.

clue.text: Baccarat or cribbage entertaining old metal band

indicators.note: entertaining means holding as a guest, so the phrase keeps the answer within it

parts.note: spans the end of the first word, the whole second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Card games played to amuse an aging heavy metal group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'metal band' suggests a rock group; it is a band of metal worn on the neck.
explanation.definitionFit: A torc is a twisted metal neck ring worn by ancient Celts, hence an old metal band.

clue.text: Second XI from Bundesliga showing personality

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
elf is German for eleven, the Bundesliga being Germany's football league

explanation.surface: A German football club's reserve team shows character.
explanation.walkthrough: XI looks like a football team, as in Second XI; it is just the number eleven, in German.
explanation.definitionFit: Your self is your individual nature and identity, which is what personality describes.

clue.text: Unpaid workers sadly lost most of revenue

indicators.note: sadly means badly, so the letters are messed up into a new order
most of a word means all except its final letter

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A charity laments that unpaid helpers cost it most of its income.
explanation.definitionFit: Volunteers are people who work by choice without pay, such as charity shop helpers.

clue.text: Crossword setters and their boss like an old chestnut

parts.note: setters write as 'we', so they are us
ED is short for editor, the boss of the setters

explanation.surface: The setters and their editor are as stale as a worn-out joke.
explanation.walkthrough: A chestnut is a stale old joke, so the definition is about being worn out.
explanation.definitionFit: Used here means second-hand or worn, hackneyed through repetition, like a joke told too often.

clue.text: Eastern practice and spicy beverage mentioned by Spooner

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of two words trade places

parts.note: chai tea is spiced Indian-style tea

explanation.surface: An Eastern custom involving spiced tea.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of chai tea and you say tai chi.
explanation.definitionFit: Tai chi is a Chinese martial art practised as slow flowing exercise, an Eastern discipline.

clue.text: Star baseball player's decoration hung by window

parts.note: the sun is a star
the catcher is the fielder behind home plate

explanation.surface: A star baseball player's ornament hangs by a window.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star' looks like an adjective for the player, but it is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A suncatcher is a piece of coloured glass or crystal hung in a window to catch and scatter light.

clue.text: Wise guy's parting words briefly interrupted by doctor

indicators.note: being interrupted means something breaks into the middle
briefly means cut short, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: so long is a farewell
MO is medical officer, an army doctor

explanation.surface: A smart alec's goodbye is cut off by a doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wise guy' suggests a know-all; here it is meant literally. SO LONG loses its G, then the doctor goes in before the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: King Solomon of the Bible is proverbial for wisdom, so a wise man is called a Solomon.

clue.text: Conductor not getting involved in dispute

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the return wire in an electrical circuit

explanation.surface: An orchestra conductor keeps out of a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: The conductor is electrical, not musical.
explanation.definitionFit: Neutral names the wire in a circuit that carries current back, and also describes an impartial party in a conflict.

clue.text: Communist right to reject books mentioning Methuselah

indicators.note: rejecting something turns it back the way it came

parts.note: RT is an abbreviation for right
the Old Testament records Methuselah, the longest-lived man in the Bible

explanation.surface: A left-winger has the right to reject books that name the puzzle's setter.
explanation.walkthrough: Methuselah is this crossword's setter, a little in-joke; the Old Testament is where the name comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: Trot is short for Trotskyist, an informal word for a hard-left communist.

clue.text: Crew of sycophants giving up time for king

indicators.note: giving up one thing for another means swapping one letter out for a different one

parts.note: toadies are flatterers
T is the abbreviation for time
R is short for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A crew of flatterers quit serving time to serve a king.
explanation.definitionFit: Roadies are the touring crew who set up equipment for bands, so they form a crew.

clue.text: Economical fee about to be deducted from £3.50

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the word reads the other way
deducting means taking away, so those letters are removed from the longer string

parts.note: taken as written
the price said in words

explanation.surface: A thrifty discount knocks a fee off a £3.50 price.
explanation.walkthrough: Spell out three fifty and the backwards fee sits in the middle: THR-EEF-IFTY.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrifty means careful with money and resources, as is someone economical.

clue.text: Pull up by space and park?

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is written from bottom to top

parts.note: to drag is to pull
an en is a printer's space

explanation.surface: Someone pulls up their car by a parking space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pull up' and 'park' summon a car, but 'up' reverses the pull. The question mark admits a park is only loosely a garden.
explanation.definitionFit: A garden can be a public park, as in botanical gardens or Kensington Gardens in London.

clue.text: Pea shoots or rocket leaves from this?

definitions.text: Pea shoots or rocket leaves from this?

parts.note: surface reading: salad greens, young pea plants and peppery rocket leaves
setter's reading: a pea shoots out of it and a rocket leaves from it

explanation.surface: A salad bowl of pea shoots or rocket leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: Shoots and leaves become verbs: the thing a pea is fired from and the thing a rocket takes off from. Rocket is the British name for arugula.
explanation.definitionFit: A launcher is any device that propels a projectile, from a pea shooter to a rocket launch pad.

clue.text: Retro graffiti unnervingly captures discontent

indicators.note: retro means backward-looking, so the letters run in the opposite direction
the phrase captures the answer, holding it within its letters

parts.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Old-school street art unsettlingly expresses dissatisfaction.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennui is weary boredom and dissatisfaction, a listless kind of discontent.

clue.text: Market leaders in zero alcohol ale stocked by boozer

indicators.note: goods stocked by a shop are held inside it

parts.note: boozer is British slang for a pub, a bar

indicators.note: the leaders of words are their opening letters

parts.note: the first letter of each word

explanation.surface: Top brands of alcohol-free beer are sold at the pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A bazaar is a market, originally a street of stalls in the Middle East.

clue.text: Duck pirate aboard the Jolly Roger

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a dialect name for a wild duck such as the smew or pintail
second meaning: Captain Hook's bosun in Peter Pan

explanation.surface: A pirate on Hook's ship ducks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' reads like a command to dodge; it is the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Smee is a regional name for some wild ducks, and Mr Smee is Captain Hook's sidekick in J M Barrie's Peter Pan.

clue.text: Old person and resistance spies abducted by Martians, allegedly

indicators.note: being abducted means being carried off and held within

parts.note: Martians are supposedly little green men
R is the symbol for electrical resistance
the CIA is the US spy agency

explanation.surface: An elderly resistance fighter and some agents are kidnapped by aliens.
explanation.definitionFit: A Mercian was an inhabitant of Mercia, an Anglo-Saxon kingdom of central England.

clue.text: What belly dancer reveals during guitar solo?

parts.note: mid means in the middle of
a riff is a short repeated guitar phrase

explanation.surface: A belly dancer shows off during a guitar break.
explanation.definitionFit: The midriff is the front of the body between chest and waist, the bare stomach a belly dancer shows.

clue.text: Toll from dictator's a little Dickensian

indicators.note: a dictator here is someone dictating, speaking words for others to write down

parts.note: a knell is the toll of a bell

explanation.surface: A bell tolls for a despot's small Dickensian victim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dictator' suggests a tyrant; here it is one who dictates. Little Nell is the heroine of Dickens's The Old Curiosity Shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Little Nell Trent is the child heroine of The Old Curiosity Shop, so Nell is a little Dickensian character.

clue.text: Controversial content to save Indy cryptic

indicators.note: something cryptic is obscure and puzzling, so the letters are scrambled into a riddle

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A self-referential plea that edgy material will save the Independent's crossword.
explanation.walkthrough: Indy is the nickname of The Independent newspaper, which ran this puzzle. A video nasty was a 1980s British term for a violent horror film banned or prosecuted.
explanation.definitionFit: Video nasties were horror films on home video that British censors condemned in the 1980s, a byword for controversial content.
